In the default envelope every message is three frames, name, headers, payload, so a peer in any language composes one with send_multipart. ZeroMQ carries messages made of frames and leaves their meaning to the application. This crate gives every message on PUSH/PULL and PUB/SUB the same three frames: the name, the headers and the payload. The layout is the Frames envelope, which every broker reads and writes unless it names another; Envelopes shows the others. The name frame is the subscription's name on the fan-out, matched as a prefix; a queue takes every message whatever its name says. The header frame is text, and an empty frame means no headers. A message of two frames, a name and a payload, reads as a message without headers, so a minimal peer can skip the middle frame. A message of one frame is what a plain ZeroMQ peer sends: that frame is the payload, whole, the name is empty and there are no headers. On the fan-out a SUB matches its prefix against that same frame, so a plain PUB's message reaches a subscription whose name prefixes it, and the handler reads the frame as it was sent, prefix included. A message of more than three frames has no place for the frames past the payload, and it surfaces on the subscription as ZmqError::Wire, naming how many frames it had. The payload frame is what the service's codec wrote, so a peer agrees on the codec only: with the default JSON codec it is the document the handler's input type deserializes from. Bytes a service already holds encoded go out through a #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] newtype, and no codec runs on them. A name frame that is not UTF-8 surfaces on the subscription as ZmqError::Wire. On DEALER/ROUTER a request has the same three frames, and its answer travels behind the requester's identity, as Identity frame shows. Peers in other languages feeds, watches and asks a service from Python peers.

frame 0: name UTF-8; the fan-out's subscribers filter on it as a prefix frame 1: headers UTF-8 "name: value" lines separated by \n; may be empty frame 2: payload the codec's output A Python peer pushes a job into a worker with pyzmq: socket.send_multipart([b"jobs", b"content-type: application/json", b'{"id": 2}']) The worker reads the jobs a Python PUSH socket sends, and pushes each result to a sink that a Python PULL socket binds. The sink reads the three frames results, the header lines and the JSON document {"id":2}. An envelope is the frame layout of a message: Frames by default, Framed for one codec document, NoOp for the payload alone, or a layout of your own. A broker reads and writes through one envelope, named with .envelope(..) on the broker: ZmqQueue::new(endpoint).envelope(NoOp). A publish policy writes through its broker's envelope, or through its own when it names one: Publish.envelope(NoOp). The envelope is a type parameter of the broker and the publisher, so the choice costs nothing per message. The built-in envelopes: Envelope Frames Headers Frames name, header lines, payload (Wire format) name: value lines Framed<Codec> name, then one JSON, CBOR or MessagePack document of the headers and the payload the document's headers map NoOp the payload alone; on the fan-out, the name and the payload none Frames is the default and the layout of earlier releases, so a service that names no envelope stays wire-compatible. Framed suits a peer that reads every message with one parser. Its JSON document follows the CloudEvents JSON format. A payload that is one JSON text travels as a value in payload, byte for byte as written: {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload":{"id":7}}. Any other payload travels as standard base64 in payload_base64: {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload_base64":"CAc="}. The CBOR and MessagePack documents carry the payload as a byte string in payload. NoOp suits a plain ZeroMQ peer, which sends and reads the payload and nothing else. A message that is not in the envelope's layout is a peer's own payload. A single frame reads as the payload, with an empty name and no headers, whichever envelope reads it. A Framed second frame that is not a document, headers and exactly one payload field with nothing beside them, reads as the payload too. A payload that looks like a document is safe: Framed always writes the payload inside a document of its own. A delivery reads its headers on the first call to headers(), and keeps them. A handler that reads no header never parses the envelope. Headers that do not read are logged against the message, and the delivery has none. NoOp carries no headers. A publish through it that carries a header fails with ZmqError::Send, naming the header and the destination. A retry copy carries the framework's retry counter in a header, so retry_after needs an envelope with headers. On DEALER/ROUTER a request read through NoOp still carries the reply-to address of the peer that asked, and a requester takes the first answer on its DEALER, with no correlation-id. An envelope of your own implements Envelope: open reads the frames a socket received, headers reads the headers out of what open kept, and seal writes a message. The test harness runs a broker in process by its type, so a test registers a broker on your envelope once: ruststream::register_testable_broker!(ZmqFanout<Bind, Spaced>);. The generated AsyncAPI document names the envelope on each server and on each message a publish position writes, with the media type of the Framed document.

A feed's PUB socket sends each tick as one name payload frame. The bridge reads it through an envelope of its own: examples/zmq_wire_envelopes.rs /// One frame: the name, a space, and the payload, the layout of many hand-written PUB sockets. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)] struct Spaced; impl Envelope for Spaced { type Head = (); const NAME: &'static str = "spaced"; const CARRIES_HEADERS: bool = false; fn open(&self, _pattern: Pattern, frames: VecDeque<Bytes>) -> Result<Opened<()>, ZmqError> { let frame = frames.into_iter().next().unwrap_or_default(); let Some(at) = frame.iter().position(|&byte| byte == b' ') else { // A frame without a space is a peer's payload, with no name. return Ok(Opened::new("", (), frame)); }; let name = std::str::from_utf8(&frame[..at]) .map_err(|_| ZmqError::Wire("the name must be UTF-8".into()))?; Ok(Opened::new(name, (), frame.slice(at + 1..))) } fn headers(_head: &()) -> Result<HeaderMap, ZmqError> { Ok(HeaderMap::new()) } fn seal( &self, _pattern: Pattern, name: &str, headers: &HeaderMap, payload: Bytes, frames: &mut Vec<Bytes>, ) -> Result<(), SealError> { if let Some((header, _)) = headers.iter().next() { return Err(SealError::new(format!( "header {header:?} has no place in the frame" ))); } frames.push([name.as_bytes(), b" ", &payload].concat().into()); Ok(()) } } Each price leaves the bridge as one JSON document on a fan-out. The header frame is UTF-8 name: value lines, read when a handler first asks; a header the frame cannot carry is refused on publish, and a malformed frame reads as no headers. Frame 1 holds one header per line, the name and the value separated by :, and lines separated by \n. A service reads and writes headers through the core's typed contract: a serde struct whose fields are the headers, parsed by Headers<T> in the handler and declared on an outgoing type with #[outgoing(headers = T)]. Nothing is guessed in either direction. A header value that is not UTF-8 has no form in a text frame, so its publish fails with ZmqError::Send, naming the header and the destination. So does a header that would read back as something else: a line break in its name or value, a : in its name, or whitespace at either end of either. A delivery reads its header frame on the first call to headers(), so a handler that reads no header never parses it. A peer's header frame that is not UTF-8, or a line without :, is logged against the message, and the message reaches the handler with no headers. Blank lines are skipped, so a peer that ends the frame with a newline interoperates. A name and a value are trimmed of surrounding whitespace on receipt. Peers in other languages composes the header frame from a Python peer.

A Python peer writes the frame by hand: socket.send_multipart([b"jobs", b"x-tenant: acme\ncontent-type: application/json", payload]) The worker reads the tenant a peer names in x-tenant and sends it on with the result. On DEALER/ROUTER a request carries correlation-id, and its answer travels behind the requester's identity with frame 0 holding reply. A requester sends the usual three frames of the default envelope from a DEALER socket, with a correlation-id line in the header frame. The responder's ROUTER puts the DEALER's identity in front of them; ZeroMQ calls that frame the routing envelope. The responder reads the identity off and gives the request a reply-to header that addresses it. The answer goes back through the ROUTER as [identity, "reply", headers, payload]. The ROUTER takes the identity frame off to route it, so the DEALER reads three frames: the literal reply, the header lines with the request's correlation-id, and the payload. The requester matches the answer to its request by that id, because frame 0 is the same on every answer. The correlation-id reaches the answer through the responder's transform. Peers in other languages asks a responder from a Python DEALER.

A Python requester: dealer.send_multipart([b"greeter", b"correlation-id: ask-1", b'{"who": "world"}']) name, headers, payload = dealer.recv_multipart() The greeter binds tcp://0.0.0.0:5557 and answers each DEALER that asks. Every watcher that dials the announcer receives its own copy of each announcement. The watcher dials, so its mount names where retry copies go, even though watch never asks for a retry. The copies go to a queue the watcher binds for itself, and the same handler reads it. Retries and dead letters covers this rule.

A fan-out stores nothing. A watcher receives what is published after its subscription has reached the publisher, and nothing from before. A watcher that starts late, or reconnects, misses the announcements in between. An announcement that matches no watcher is dropped without an error. A service that announces to its own subscription loses nothing to this: its publisher reads that subscription's filter before the first send.

A watcher reads at most read_ahead deliveries ahead of its handler, 1000 by default. Past that it stops reading, and the socket buffers fill. The publisher then waits for the slowest watcher whose prefix matches. So a slow watcher slows the announcer down instead of losing announcements.

A retry copy on a fan-out is a publish like any other: it reaches every subscription whose prefix matches. On a fan-out the service binds, a copy goes back to the whole audience the original had. A dead-letter name on the same endpoint matches the prefix too: jobs.dead arrives on jobs. and is handled again. A fan-out's dead letters go to an endpoint of their own.

The in-process mode applies the prefix rule; late joiners and back-pressure exist only on real sockets. Testing a ZeroMQ service covers both modes.
This guide installs ruststream-zeromq, runs a first worker and feeds it from a peer in another process.

Any process that speaks ZMTP can push jobs to the worker. A message is three frames: the name, the headers and the payload (Wire format). This Python peer uses pyzmq: push_job.py import json import zmq push = zmq.Context().socket(zmq.PUSH) push.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555") push.send_multipart([b"jobs", b"", json.dumps({"id": 1, "items": 3}).encode()]) push.close(linger=1000) Run it from another terminal: python3 push_job.py The service logs job taken with the job's id and item count. A warning follows it: ack / nack failed, acknowledgement is not supported by this broker. ZeroMQ has no acknowledgement on the wire, so the job counts as done once the worker reads it (Acknowledgement). Ctrl+C stops it. The peer can be a RustStream service too: Pipelines with PUSH/PULL builds one that pushes its results to another.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, pushes a job and checks how take_job settled it. The broker runs in process there, so the tests open no socket: cargo test Testing a ZeroMQ service walks through the harness and the same test over real sockets.

A service on a ZeroMQ binding opens its sockets and writes its own receive loop. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: pyzmq or libzmq RustStream ctx.socket(zmq.PULL) and bind ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(..)) and a #[subscriber] handler connect ZmqEndpoint::connect; the side is part of the broker's type a recv_multipart loop the handler, called once per message decoding the payload frame the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec send_multipart a reply or an Out parameter, sent through a publish policy setsockopt(zmq.SUBSCRIBE, prefix) the subscription name on ZmqFanout (Broadcast with PUB/SUB) REQ and REP ZmqRpc over DEALER and ROUTER (Request and reply) tcp://*:5555 tcp://0.0.0.0:5555 inproc:// TestApp for tests; ipc:// between processes on one host SNDHWM and RCVHWM read_ahead (Running in production) a zmq.Poller over several sockets one subscription per socket, each on a task of its own

This guide connects a RustStream service to peers written in other languages: a PUSH that feeds it, a SUB that reads its announcements, and a DEALER that asks it. The peers here use pyzmq, the Python binding of libzmq. A peer in C, C++ or another language composes the same frames with its own binding.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_zeromq::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Job { id: u64, items: u32, } /// Announced on the fan-out, under a name a `jobs.` subscriber matches. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "jobs.done")] struct JobDone { id: u64, items: u32, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct ScoreRequest { customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } // No destination of its own: the ROUTER addresses each answer per request. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Score { customer: u64, approved: bool, } #[subscriber("jobs", reply)] async fn work(job: &Job) -> JobDone { tracing::info!(job.id, job.items, "job worked"); JobDone { id: job.id, items: job.items, } } #[subscriber("score", reply("reply"))] async fn score(request: &ScoreRequest) -> Score { tracing::info!(request.customer, request.amount_cents, "scoring"); Score { customer: request.customer, approved: request.amount_cents <= 50_000, } } /// The service on the three endpoints it binds: jobs in, announcements out, requests answered. fn service(jobs: &str, events: &str, scoring: &str) -> RustStream { let events = ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(events)).bindable(); const DESTINATION: &'static str = "jobs.done"; } impl MessageHeaders for JobDone { type Contract = NoHeaders; } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct ScoreRequest { customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Score { customer: u64, approved: bool, } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no name by hand: the ROUTER addresses each answer per request. impl OutgoingDestination for Score { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Score { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Work; impl Handle<Job, JobDone> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<JobDone, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, job.items, "job worked"); ready(Ok(JobDone { id: job.id, items: job.items, })) } } struct ScoreIt; impl Handle<ScoreRequest, Score> for ScoreIt { fn handle( &self, request: &ScoreRequest, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Score, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(request.customer, request.amount_cents, "scoring"); ready(Ok(Score { customer: request.customer, approved: request.amount_cents <= 50_000, })) } } /// The service on the three endpoints it binds: jobs in, announcements out, requests answered. fn service(jobs: &str, events: &str, scoring: &str) -> RustStream { let events = ZmqFanout::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(events)).bindable(); let announce = events.bind(ZmqFanoutPublish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(jobs)), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).reply().build()) .out_reply(announce) }) .with_broker(events, |b| b) .with_broker(ZmqRpc::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind(scoring)), |b| { b.include(subscriber("score", ScoreIt).reply().to("reply").build()) .out_reply(ZmqRpcPublish) .transform(ReplyToRequester) .out_retry(ZmqRpcPublish) .to("score.retry") }) } fn app() -> RustStream { service( "tcp://0.0.0.0:5555", "tcp://0.0.0.0:5556", "tcp://0.0.0.0:5557", ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The service binds three endpoints. jobs on port 5555 is a ZmqQueue that takes the jobs a PUSH sends. Each worked job is announced as jobs.done on the ZmqFanout on port 5556. score on port 5557 answers requests on a ZmqRpc; ReplyToRequester is the transform of Request and reply.

Every message is three frames in the default envelope (Wire format): frame 0: name UTF-8; on PUB/SUB also what a subscriber's prefix is matched against frame 1: headers UTF-8 "name: value" lines separated by \n; may be empty frame 2: payload what the codec wrote; JSON by default A peer that sends two frames, the name and the payload, sends a message with no headers. A peer that sends one frame, as a plain ZeroMQ application does, sends that frame as the payload, with an empty name; on PUB/SUB the prefix is matched against it. A message of more than three frames fails the delivery with ZmqError::Wire. A peer that reads a single frame, or one JSON document per message, is served by another envelope on the broker. A blank line in the header frame is skipped, so a line that ends with a newline is fine. A name that is not UTF-8 fails the delivery with ZmqError::Wire. A header frame that is not UTF-8, or a header line with no :, is logged, and the message reaches the handler with no headers. The service checks the headers it publishes, so that each reads back unchanged: a header that is not text, holds a line break, has a : in its name, or starts or ends with whitespace fails the publish with ZmqError::Send, naming the header and the destination.

push.py import json import zmq push = zmq.Context().socket(zmq.PUSH) push.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555") push.send_multipart([ b"jobs", b"content-type: application/json", json.dumps({"id": 1, "items": 3}).encode(), ]) push.close(linger=1000) The name frame is jobs, but a bound PULL takes every message pushed to it, whatever its name.
documents.s: A PUSH that feeds the service

documents.t: watch.py import json import zmq sub = zmq.Context().socket(zmq.SUB) sub.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5556") sub.setsockopt(zmq.SUBSCRIBE, b"jobs.") name, headers, payload = sub.recv_multipart() print(name.decode(), json.loads(payload)) The subscription is a prefix of the name frame, as it is for a RustStream watcher (Broadcast with PUB/SUB). A SUB receives the announcements published after it has joined the fan-out, and none from before. Start watch.py, run push.py, and run it again a second later, so that an announcement is published after the SUB has joined. watch.py prints the first announcement it receives and exits: jobs.done {'id': 1, 'items': 3}.
documents.s: A SUB that reads the announcements

documents.t: ask.py import json import zmq dealer = zmq.Context().socket(zmq.DEALER) dealer.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5557") dealer.send_multipart([ b"score", b"correlation-id: 42", json.dumps({"customer": 3, "amount_cents": 1250}).encode(), ]) name, headers, payload = dealer.recv_multipart() print(name, headers, json.loads(payload)) A requester on the other side of ZmqRpc is a DEALER, and it sends the three frames. The ROUTER adds the DEALER's identity in front of them and the reply-to header to the request. The answer comes back as three frames, and frame 0 is the literal reply (Identity frame). The headers carry the request's correlation-id, so a DEALER with several requests in flight matches each answer to its request: b'reply' b'correlation-id: 42' {'customer': 3, 'approved': True}
documents.s: A DEALER that asks the service

documents.t: The payload frame is whatever the codec wrote, so a peer agrees with the service on the codec, not on Rust types. JSON is the default; msgpack and cbor are features of ruststream. Bytes the peer framed itself pass through untouched in a #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] newtype (Wire format).

The client greets every peer with ZMTP 3.0. libzmq 4 speaks ZMTP 3.1 and accepts a 3.0 peer, and the zeromq client is tested against libzmq. The handshake uses the NULL mechanism, so a peer joins without credentials. Traffic is plain: Running in production covers where to run it.

With the asyncapi feature, the generated document tells a peer how to join each channel (AsyncAPI). The server reports the transport, the address and the side this service takes. A channel reports its socket pair and, on PUSH/PULL and PUB/SUB, nameFrame: the frame 0 a peer sends or subscribes with. A responder's reply channel points at the reply-to header instead of an address.
documents.s: The contract in the generated document

documents.t: The in-process test pushes a job as a peer would and checks the announcement published on jobs.done. The second test runs the service over real sockets with TestApp::start_live. A raw zeromq DEALER plays the foreign peer: it composes the request frames by hand and checks the three frames of the answer. The responder binds a socket path of the test's own, so parallel runs never meet.

This guide builds the pipeline of the ZeroMQ guide: a ventilator pushes jobs, workers compete for them, and a sink collects the results. The example has two services. The worker takes jobs from the ventilator and pushes a result for each to the sink. The sink collects the results in batches. The ventilator is any peer that pushes jobs, such as the Python peer of Getting started.

The stable side of a connection binds, and the side that comes and goes dials. In a pipeline the ventilator and the sink are stable, so they bind. The workers dial both, and one more worker process is one more dial. ZmqEndpoint::bind and ZmqEndpoint::connect state the side. The side is part of the broker's type: a broker built on connect is a ZmqQueue<Connect>. It decides what the broker may publish and where a retry copy can go, so a mistake is caught at compile time or at startup, not in production.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Job { id: u64, items: u32, } /// What the sink collects: one result per job. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "results")] struct Done { id: u64, items: u32, } #[subscriber("jobs", reply)] async fn work(job: &Job) -> Done { tracing::info!(job.id, job.items, "job worked"); Done { id: job.id, items: job.items, } } src/main.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Job { id: u64, items: u32, } /// What the sink collects: one result per job. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Done { id: u64, items: u32, } // `#[outgoing(name = "results")]` by hand: the type names the subscription it is pushed to. impl OutgoingDestination for Done { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "results"; } impl MessageHeaders for Done { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Work; impl Handle<Job, Done> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Done, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, job.items, "job worked"); ready(Ok(Done { id: job.id, items: job.items, })) } } work takes a job and returns a Done. Done names its destination itself, results, so the subscriber clause carries a bare reply. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The sink listens; every worker dials it and only pushes there. let sink = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://sink:5558")).bindable(); // The retry copies come back through a queue this worker binds for itself. let retries = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5559")).bindable(); let (results, retried_results) = (sink.bind(Publish), sink.bind(Publish)); let copies = retries.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "ventilator", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5557")), |b| { b.include(work) .out_reply(results) .out_retry(copies) .to("jobs") }, ) .with_broker_labeled("retries", retries, |b| { b.include(work).out_reply(retried_results) }) .with_broker_labeled("sink", sink, |b| b) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { // The sink listens; every worker dials it and only pushes there. let sink = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://sink:5558")).bindable(); // The retry copies come back through a queue this worker binds for itself. let retries = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5559")).bindable(); let (results, retried_results) = (sink.bind(Publish), sink.bind(Publish)); let copies = retries.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "ventilator", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://ventilator:5557")), |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).reply().build()) .out_reply(results) .out_retry(copies) .to("jobs") }, ) .with_broker_labeled("retries", retries, |b| { b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).reply().build()) .out_reply(retried_results) }) .with_broker_labeled("sink", sink, |b| b) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The ventilator broker dials the ventilator, and its subscription reads the jobs. Workers that dial one ventilator compete: PUSH hands each job to one worker, in turn. The results leave through a second broker, sink, which dials the sink. bindable() turns a broker into one that publish policies can be bound to, and sink.bind(Publish) is a policy that publishes through it. .out_reply(results) sends every Done there. The worker cannot reply through the ventilator broker: the ventilator only sends, so the broker refuses every publish once its subscription has dialed. Replies covers the refusals. A subscription that dials also names where its retry copies go, even when its handler never asks for a retry. Here they go to retries, a queue the worker binds for itself, and the same handler reads it. A copy carries the name jobs, the name of the subscription that takes it back. Retries and dead letters covers retries in full.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Done { id: u64, items: u32, } #[subscriber("results")] async fn collect(results: &[Done]) -> HandlerOutcome { let items: u32 = results.iter().map(|done| done.items).sum(); tracing::info!(results = results.len(), items, "results collected"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("sink", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5558")), |b| { // At most 32 results per call. b.include(collect.batch(nonzero!(32))) }, ) } src/main.rs use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Done { id: u64, items: u32, } struct Collect; impl Handle<[Done]> for Collect { fn handle( &self, results: &[Done], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let items: u32 = results.iter().map(|done| done.items).sum(); tracing::info!(results = results.len(), items, "results collected"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("sink", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5558")), |b| { // At most 32 results per call. b.include(subscriber("results", Collect).batch(nonzero!(32)).build()) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The sink binds the address the workers dial. A bound PULL socket takes whatever any worker pushes to it, so one subscription reads the results of every worker. collect takes a slice, so it receives batches. A batch closes once it holds 32 results, or 20 ms after its first result, whichever comes first. The frames on the wire do not change: the batch is gathered on the sink's side.

PUSH and PULL do not look at the name frame. A bound queue hands its subscription every message pushed to it, whatever the name says. So a second kind of work, such as reports next to jobs, gets an endpoint of its own and a broker of its own. A second subscription on a bound endpoint is refused at startup, and the error names both subscriptions.
documents.s: One kind of work per endpoint

documents.t: PUSH hands messages to the attached workers in turn and does not read a key. Two jobs of one customer may run on two workers at the same time. A handler that must see one customer's jobs in order runs in one worker process. Inside one process, workers at the mount site runs several deliveries of a handler at once. A ZeroMQ message carries no key, so lanes keyed with by_key take its deliveries in turn.

Each example file holds a test that starts its service with TestApp::start. The worker's test pushes a job as the ventilator would and reads the result published to results on the sink broker. The sink's test pushes three results at once and checks that collect received them as one batch. Testing a ZeroMQ service covers the harness.
ZeroMQ has no server between services, so the deployment decides what a broker would otherwise decide: who listens, in which order services start, and how far a slow consumer buffers.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use std::env; use std::num::NonZeroUsize; use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; /// What the deployment decides: where the worker listens, where the sink is, and how far a /// subscription reads ahead of its handler. struct Settings { jobs: String, sink: String, read_ahead: NonZeroUsize, } impl Settings { fn from_env() -> Self { Self::from_vars(|name| env::var(name).ok()) } fn from_vars(var: impl Fn(&str) -> Option<String>) -> Self { Self { jobs: var("JOBS_BIND").unwrap_or_else(|| "tcp://0.0.0.0:5555".to_owned()), sink: var("SINK_ADDR").unwrap_or_else(|| "tcp://sink:5558".to_owned()), read_ahead: var("ZMQ_READ_AHEAD") .and_then(|value| value.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(nonzero!(1000_usize)), } } } src/main.rs use std::env; use std::num::NonZeroUsize; use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; /// What the deployment decides: where the worker listens, where the sink is, and how far a /// subscription reads ahead of its handler. struct Settings { jobs: String, sink: String, read_ahead: NonZeroUsize, } impl Settings { fn from_env() -> Self { Self::from_vars(|name| env::var(name).ok()) } fn from_vars(var: impl Fn(&str) -> Option<String>) -> Self { Self { jobs: var("JOBS_BIND").unwrap_or_else(|| "tcp://0.0.0.0:5555".to_owned()), sink: var("SINK_ADDR").unwrap_or_else(|| "tcp://sink:5558".to_owned()), read_ahead: var("ZMQ_READ_AHEAD") .and_then(|value| value.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(nonzero!(1000_usize)), } } } The endpoints and the read-ahead bound are the service's whole ZeroMQ configuration. Settings reads them from the environment the deployment sets, with a default for each. from_vars takes the lookup as a function, so a test passes its own values without touching the process environment. tcp://10.0.0.5:5555 listens on one. ipc:///run/jobs.sock is a Unix socket for services on one host. The side is part of the broker's type, so the deployment chooses the address and the code chooses the side.

A subscription that binds opens its port at startup, and a port another process holds fails the start with ZmqError::Endpoint. A subscription that dials waits for its peer to listen. The client retries the connection for up to 30 seconds, then the start fails with ZmqError::Endpoint, naming the address. So a service that dials may start before the peer it dials, as long as the peer listens within that window. A publisher on the bind side listens from the moment the service starts, so a peer that dials it connects before the first message. A publisher that dials attaches on its first publish. A send with no peer attached retries for five seconds, then fails with ZmqError::Send, naming the destination.

A publisher that dials its peer dials again once that peer has gone, and reaches it when it is back. A queue publisher learns of the loss from a failed send: the message sent into the dead connection is lost, the next publish returns ZmqError::Send, and the one after it dials anew. A fan-out publisher learns of it from its socket and dials on its next publish. A fan-out subscription that dials is dialed again by the client. A subscription that dials a PUSH peer keeps the connection it opened, so after that peer restarts it receives nothing until the service restarts too.

A subscription reads at most read_ahead deliveries ahead of its handler, 1000 by default. Past that bound it stops reading, the socket buffers fill, and the sender waits. So a slow handler slows the sender down instead of growing the memory of the service. On PUB/SUB the waiting sender is the publisher, held back by its slowest matching subscriber. The bound is set per broker, here from ZMQ_READ_AHEAD.

The client negotiates the NULL mechanism: peers connect without credentials, and traffic travels as plain bytes. A service therefore runs inside a network it trusts, or inside a tunnel: a VPN, WireGuard, or an SSH tunnel. The generated AsyncAPI document reports each endpoint's host and port without credentials (Server).

On shutdown the service stops its subscriptions and closes its sockets. A publisher handed out earlier then fails with ZmqError::NotConnected instead of sending into nothing. A queue publish is safe to cancel. A fan-out publish, a reply and a request are not, so give up through a timeout, not a select! arm (Cancellation).

The tests build Settings with from_vars. One checks the defaults of an empty environment. The other starts the configured service under TestApp::start and checks that a result reaches the sink. The in-process mode opens no socket, so the addresses need not exist.

This guide answers requests on DEALER/ROUTER and asks another service from inside a handler. The example has two services. The scoring service answers whether an order amount is approved for a customer. The checkout service asks it about each order it takes.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_zeromq::rpc::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct ScoreRequest { customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } // No destination of its own: the ROUTER addresses each answer per request. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Score { customer: u64, approved: bool, } // The answer goes to the peer that asked, so the clause's name is only the fallback. #[subscriber("score", reply("reply"))] async fn score(request: &ScoreRequest) -> Result<Score, HandlerOutcome> { if request.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(request.customer, "a request without an amount, dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } tracing::info!(request.customer, request.amount_cents, "scoring"); Ok(Score { customer: request.customer, approved: request.amount_cents <= 50_000, }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The responder is the stable side: it binds, and every requester dials it. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("scoring", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqRpc::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5557")), |b| { // A responder addresses no retry copies, so the mount names where they go. b.include(score) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ReplyToRequester) .out_retry(Publish) .to("score.retry") }, ) } src/main.rs use ruststream_zeromq::rpc::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct ScoreRequest { customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Score { customer: u64, approved: bool, } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no name by hand: the ROUTER addresses each answer per request. impl OutgoingDestination for Score { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Score { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct ScoreIt; impl Handle<ScoreRequest, Score> for ScoreIt { fn handle( &self, request: &ScoreRequest, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Score, HandlerOutcome>> { if request.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(request.customer, "a request without an amount, dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(request.customer, request.amount_cents, "scoring"); ready(Ok(Score { customer: request.customer, approved: request.amount_cents <= 50_000, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The responder is the stable side: it binds, and every requester dials it. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("scoring", "0.1.0")).with_broker( ZmqRpc::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5557")), |b| { // The answer goes to the peer that asked, so the `to` name is only the fallback. // A responder addresses no retry copies, so the mount names where they go. b.include(subscriber("score", ScoreIt).reply().to("reply").build()) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ReplyToRequester) .out_retry(Publish) .to("score.retry") }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } ZmqRpc is the DEALER/ROUTER pattern. The responder is the stable side, so it binds, and every requester dials it. score is an ordinary reply handler: it returns the answer, or drops a request without an amount. A ROUTER socket knows which peer sent each request. It stamps that peer on the request as a reply-to header, and the answer must go there. So Score declares no destination of its own, and reply("reply") names only a fallback. The transform below replaces it for each request. A responder names where its retry copies go: .out_retry(Publish).to("score.retry"). A copy of a request has no address of its own, so .out_retry(..) without .to(..) does not compile, and a mount with no retry slot is refused at startup. A responder also takes no batches: .batch(..) on it does not compile, because each answer goes to its own peer.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Answers at the `reply-to` address the ROUTER stamped on the request, under the request's /// `correlation-id`. #[derive(Clone)] struct ReplyToRequester; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ReplyToRequester { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(reply_to) = cx.headers().get_shared("reply-to") && let Ok(reply_to) = Str::try_from(reply_to) { out.set_name(reply_to); } if let Some(correlation) = cx.headers().get_shared("correlation-id") { out.headers_mut() .insert(Str::from_static("correlation-id"), correlation); } } } src/main.rs /// Answers at the `reply-to` address the ROUTER stamped on the request, under the request's /// `correlation-id`. #[derive(Clone)] struct ReplyToRequester; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ReplyToRequester { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(reply_to) = cx.headers().get_shared("reply-to") && let Ok(reply_to) = Str::try_from(reply_to) { out.set_name(reply_to); } if let Some(correlation) = cx.headers().get_shared("correlation-id") { out.headers_mut() .insert(Str::from_static("correlation-id"), correlation); } } } ReplyToRequester is a publish transform on the reply. It reads the request's reply-to header and sends the answer there. It also copies the request's correlation-id, which the requester matches the answer by. It declares Destination = Names, because it chooses the destination. A transform may do that only where the reply type declares none, so a named reply type and this transform do not compile together. An answer to a peer that has gone is refused with an error naming its address. The responder learns that its answer arrived nowhere; on a fan-out, an unmatched message is dropped without a word.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use std::time::Duration; use ruststream::OutgoingMessage; use ruststream_zeromq::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; /// How long one request waits for its answer. const ASK_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); /// When the order is asked about again after the scoring service did not answer. const ASK_AGAIN: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Serialize)] struct ScoreRequest { customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Deserialize)] struct Score { approved: bool, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn check(order: &Order, Out(scoring): Out<impl RequestReply>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(request) = serde_json::to_vec(&ScoreRequest { customer: order.customer, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, }) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("score", request.as_slice()); let answer = match scoring.request(request, ASK_TIMEOUT).await { Ok(answer) => answer, Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "no score, asking again later"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(ASK_AGAIN); } }; let Ok(score) = serde_json::from_slice::<Score>(answer.payload()) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; tracing::info!(order.id, score.approved, "order checked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The scoring service binds; every requester dials it. let scoring = ZmqRpc::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://scoring:5557")).bindable(); let ask = scoring.bind(ZmqRpcPublish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { b.include(check) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .out(DefaultSlot, ask) }, ) .with_broker(scoring, |b| b) } src/main.rs use std::time::Duration; use ruststream::OutgoingMessage; use ruststream_zeromq::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; /// How long one request waits for its answer. const ASK_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); /// When the order is asked about again after the scoring service did not answer. const ASK_AGAIN: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Serialize)] struct ScoreRequest { customer: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Deserialize)] struct Score { approved: bool, } struct Check; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Check where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: RequestReply>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let request = serde_json::to_vec(&ScoreRequest { customer: order.customer, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, }) .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("score", request.as_slice()); let answer = match outs.get(DefaultSlot).request(request, ASK_TIMEOUT).await { Ok(answer) => answer, Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "no score, asking again later"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(ASK_AGAIN)); } }; let score = serde_json::from_slice::<Score>(answer.payload()) .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; tracing::info!(order.id, score.approved, "order checked"); Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The scoring service binds; every requester dials it. let scoring = ZmqRpc::new(ZmqEndpoint::connect("tcp://scoring:5557")).bindable(); let ask = scoring.bind(ZmqRpcPublish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Check).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .out(DefaultSlot, ask) }, ) .with_broker(scoring, |b| b) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } check takes an Out<impl RequestReply> parameter, and the mount site binds it to a ZmqRpc policy with .out(DefaultSlot, ask). The scoring broker dials the scoring service and has no subscription; it only asks. request sends the request over a DEALER socket of its own and returns the answer that carries the same correlation-id. check encodes the request and decodes the answer itself, with the JSON the scoring service reads and writes.

A request that gets no answer in ASK_TIMEOUT fails with ZmqError::RequestTimeout. check then returns retry_after(ASK_AGAIN), and the order comes back ten seconds later. max_attempts caps the tries at three. This is the Lazy Pirate pattern of the ZeroMQ guide, with the framework keeping the count. A request that timed out may still have reached the responder, so a request must be safe to send twice. Neither request nor a reply publish is safe to cancel. A handler gives up through the request's timeout, not through a select! arm (Cancellation).

The scoring service's tests send requests as a requester's DEALER would and check how score settled them. The checkout test runs with no scoring service in process, so its request times out. It checks that check asked for a retry, and that the copy came back after ASK_AGAIN with a retry count of one. The clock is paused, so the timeout and the delay pass at once. Testing a ZeroMQ service covers the harness.

This guide retries a message later, caps the attempts and parks what fails on a dead-letter queue. ZeroMQ delivers a message at most once and stores nothing. A message that a handler fails on is gone unless the service publishes it again. The framework does that: the mount site declares the cap and where the copies go, and each copy carries a retry count in a header. The example is a billing service with two workers. The job worker retries a failed job into its own queue. The invoice worker parks a failed invoice on a queue of its own, for a person to look at.

ack and nack have nothing to tell the socket: ZeroMQ has no acknowledgement. Each of them reports AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning. A plain retry with no cap therefore brings nothing back, and the handler is not called again. A retry that must happen goes through a copy, as below.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use std::time::Duration; use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; /// How long a failed job waits before its next delivery. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Job { id: u64, } #[subscriber("jobs")] async fn work(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { match run(job) { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the job failed, retrying later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF) } } } src/main.rs use std::time::Duration; use ruststream_zeromq::queue::prelude::*; use serde::Deserialize; /// How long a failed job waits before its next delivery. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Job { id: u64, } struct Work; impl Handle<Job> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(run(job).map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the job failed, retrying later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF) })) } } A job that fails asks for another try in 30 seconds with retry_after. The runtime waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the delivery, its payload and headers as they arrived. The copy waits in the memory of the service, so a process that stops before the delay is over loses it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Invoice { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber("invoices")] async fn send_invoice(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { if invoice.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(invoice.id, "an invoice without an amount, parking it"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, invoice.amount_cents, "invoice sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Keeps the invoices nobody could send, for a person to look at. #[subscriber("invoices.dead")] async fn park(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(invoice.id, "invoice parked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Invoice { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct SendInvoice; impl Handle<Invoice> for SendInvoice { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if invoice.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(invoice.id, "an invoice without an amount, parking it"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, invoice.amount_cents, "invoice sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Keeps the invoices nobody could send, for a person to look at. struct Park; impl Handle<Invoice> for Park { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(invoice.id, "invoice parked"); ready(Ok(())) } } An invoice without an amount cannot be sent, and sending it again changes nothing. send_invoice returns retry, and the mount site turns that into a dead letter. park reads the dead letters and logs each one.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let dead = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5561")).bindable(); let parked = dead.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "jobs", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // Five deliveries at most, the first one included; the copies return to this queue. b.include(work) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .out_retry(Publish) }, ) .with_broker_labeled( "invoices", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")), |b| { // A failed invoice leaves for the second queue, under the name it is read by. b.include(send_invoice) .dead_letter("invoices.dead") .out_retry(parked) }, ) .with_broker_labeled("dead", dead, |b| b.include(park)) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { let dead = ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5561")).bindable(); let parked = dead.bind(Publish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker_labeled( "jobs", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5555")), |b| { // Five deliveries at most, the first one included; the copies return to this queue. b.include(subscriber("jobs", Work).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .out_retry(Publish) }, ) .with_broker_labeled( "invoices", ZmqQueue::new(ZmqEndpoint::bind("tcp://0.0.0.0:5556")), |b| { // A failed invoice leaves for the second queue, under the name it is read by. b.include(subscriber("invoices", SendInvoice).build()) .dead_letter("invoices.dead") .out_retry(parked) }, ) .with_broker_labeled("dead", dead, |b| { b.include(subscriber("invoices.dead", Park).build()) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one job, the first included. ZMTP has no delivery counter, so the framework counts through its x-ruststream-retry-count header, and the cap holds wherever the copies travel. The fifth delivery of a failing job is not retried; with no dead-letter destination it is dropped with a warning that names the subscription. out_retry picks the publisher the copies leave through. The jobs queue is bound by this service, so .out_retry(Publish) sends each copy back into it, and whichever job worker is free takes it. The invoice mount declares dead_letter("invoices.dead") and no cap, so every failed invoice goes straight there. A dead letter is a publish like any other, and a bound queue takes only its own subscription's name. So the dead letters leave through parked, a policy on the dead broker, and park reads them there. The retry copies of a mount leave through the same publisher, so a mount trades its retries for its dead letters. A mount that wants both keeps its retries on its own queue and leaves dead-lettering out.

A worker that dials a ventilator cannot send a copy back: the ventilator only sends. Its mount names where the copies go, with .out_retry(policy).to("jobs") over a queue the worker binds for itself, and mounts the same handler on that queue. A mount that binds .out_retry(policy) and names no destination does not compile. A mount that binds no retry slot is refused at startup. out_retry shows this mount, and Pipelines with PUSH/PULL uses it.

The tests run the app in process. The job test starts on a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets 30 seconds pass at once. It checks five deliveries and a last copy that carries the retry count 4. The invoice test checks that the invoice reached park after one delivery. Testing a ZeroMQ service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, in process or over real sockets on the loopback. The service under test is a worker. It takes jobs on a queue it binds and announces each finished job as jobs.done on a fan-out it binds. A job whose input has not been uploaded yet is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a held job is dropped. The app is built by service(jobs, events), so a test chooses the addresses and main uses the production ones. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-zeromq in [dev-dependencies].

No socket is opened, and the addresses are never bound. The test addresses a broker by its production type: tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() is the queue this service binds, and tb.broker::<ZmqFanout>() the fan-out. A broker this service dials is tb.broker::<ZmqQueue<Connect>>(), and two brokers of one type are told apart by the labels of with_broker_labeled, through tb.broker_named(..). The test's job arrives the way a peer in another process pushes it. publish returns once the handler and its announcement have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled, and what was published on jobs.done. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the test over sockets below runs it too.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_job_without_its_input_is_held() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let job = Job { id: 8, uploaded: false, }; tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>().message(&job).publish().await?; tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() .subscriber("jobs") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The clock is paused: a minute of HOLD passes at once. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; let queue = tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>(); assert_eq!( queue.subscriber("jobs").outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack] ); queue .published::<Job>("jobs") .assert_called(3) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "2"); tb.broker::<ZmqFanout>() .published::<JobDone>("jobs.done") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_job_without_its_input_is_held() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let job = Job { id: 8, uploaded: false, }; tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>().message(&job).publish().await?; tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>() .subscriber("jobs") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The clock is paused: a minute of HOLD passes at once. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; let queue = tb.broker::<ZmqQueue>(); assert_eq!( queue.subscriber("jobs").outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack] ); queue .published::<Job>("jobs") .assert_called(3) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "2"); tb.broker::<ZmqFanout>() .published::<JobDone>("jobs.done") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } The test starts on a paused clock, and advance moves it forward. A minute of HOLD costs nothing. ZeroMQ stores nothing, so retry_after publishes a copy of the job to its queue when the delay ends. The copy carries the retry count in a header, and published shows it on jobs next to the test's own job. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so nothing is published after it. Each held delivery is recorded as Outcome::Nack.
documents.s: A delay, without waiting for it

documents.t: The in-process mode carries the frames a socket carries, and routes them by the pattern's rule: A queue that binds takes whatever a peer pushes to it; subscriptions that dial take a peer's messages in turn. A fan-out delivers to every subscription whose name is a prefix of the message's name. A request reaches the responder, and its answer reaches the peer that asked. A publish to an endpoint the service dials, or binds with no subscription, leaves for another process: the test reads it with published. The socket's refusals hold in process too, in the socket's words. A publish a bound queue would hand back to its own subscription is refused, and so is a second subscription on a bound endpoint. ack and nack report AckError::Unsupported, as on a socket, so a handler that settles by a plain retry fails its test. Delivery channels have no bound in process. Back-pressure, the read_ahead bound, late fan-out subscribers, the five-second wait for a peer and reconnection exist only on real sockets.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn over_loopback_sockets() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // Port zero: the system picks a free port, so parallel tests never collide. let tb = TestApp::start_live(service("tcp://127.0.0.1:0", "tcp://127.0.0.1:0")).await?; a_job_is_worked_and_announced(tb).await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn over_loopback_sockets() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // Port zero: the system picks a free port, so parallel tests never collide. let tb = TestApp::start_live(service("tcp://127.0.0.1:0", "tcp://127.0.0.1:0")).await?; a_job_is_worked_and_announced(tb).await } TestApp::start_live starts the same app over real ZMTP sockets. ZeroMQ needs no server, so the test binds loopback ports and runs in every cargo test. Port zero lets the system pick a free port, so tests that run in parallel never collide. The test's job leaves through the broker's own publisher and crosses a real socket. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. cargo test
